title: Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 1: Security and Risk Management: Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance.

blocks.text: Legal Frameworks and Computer Crime Laws

items: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) — Primary U.S. federal computer crime law
FISMA — Requires security for U.S. federal government systems
Computer Security Act of 1987 — Established NIST security role for federal systems
EU GDPR — Comprehensive data protection for EU residents
Criminal vs. Civil vs. Administrative law — Different burdens of proof

blocks.text: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) — 18 U.S.C. § 1030: From Chapple: Section 1030(a)(2) describes the misdemeanor act of intentionally accessing a computer without or in excess of authorization and obtaining information from a protected computer. Key amendments to the CFAA:

items: Extended coverage from "federal interest" computers to any computer used in interstate commerce
Added prohibition against creating any type of malicious code
Allowed for imprisonment regardless of whether damage was intended

blocks.text: FISMA (Federal Information Security Modernization Act): Extends the Computer Security Act of 1987. Requires all U.S. federal government agencies to implement information security programs. Legal Systems:

items: Copyright — Protects original creative works (automatic upon creation)
Trademark — Protects brand identity (logos, names, slogans)
Patent — Protects inventions and processes (20-year term)
Trade Secret — Protects proprietary business information (no registration required)
Licensing — Defines terms of use for software and content

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Copyright is AUTOMATIC upon creation — you don't need to register it (though registration strengthens legal claims). Patents MUST be registered and provide the strongest protection but expire after 20 years. Trade secrets have no expiration but lose protection if disclosed. The Coca-Cola formula is a classic trade secret example — it could have been patented but would have expired decades ago.

items: GDPR — EU data protection; requires consent; right to be forgotten
HIPAA — U.S. healthcare data protection (PHI)
GLBA — U.S. financial data protection
PCI DSS — Payment card industry security standard
COPPA — U.S. children's online privacy protection
Lawfulness, fairness, transparency
Purpose limitation
Data minimization
Accuracy
Storage limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
Accountability

blocks.text: HIPAA applies to healthcare providers, health insurers, health information clearinghouses, and business associates that handle Protected Health Information (PHI). From Chapple: "HIPAA defines PHI much more broadly than most expect. Employers that provide health insurance may handle PHI, so HIPAA applies." PCI DSS is mandatory for any entity that processes payment card transactions. From Destination CISSP: "Failure to comply with PCI DSS can lead to fines, loss of card processing privileges, and reputational damage." California SB 1386 implemented the first statewide data breach notification requirement. All but three U.S. states eventually followed with similar laws. Quick-Reference: Key Legal Acts and Regulations

rows: Internal controls, CEO/CFO certification, audit trails, whistleblower protection
PHI protection, breach notification (60 days), Business Associate Agreements
Healthcare providers, insurers, clearinghouses, business associates
Financial Privacy Rule, Safeguards Rule, Pretexting Protection
Parental consent required before collecting data from children under 13
12 requirements: firewalls, encryption, access control, testing, policy
Consent, right to erasure, 72-hour breach notification, DPO, data minimization
Any organization processing EU residents' data
Risk-based security programs for federal systems, annual reviews
Protect student educational records; parental consent for disclosure
Criminalizes unauthorized access to computer systems

blocks.text: Import/Export Controls and Trans-Border Data Flow

items: EAR (Export Administration Regulations) — Controls dual-use technology exports
ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations) — Controls defense-related exports
Wassenaar Arrangement — Multilateral export control agreement
Encryption technology is subject to export restrictions
Trans-border data flow must comply with both source and destination country laws

blocks.text: Export controls affect information security because strong encryption technology is classified as a controlled item. Organizations that develop or distribute encryption products must comply with export regulations. The Wassenaar Arrangement is a voluntary export control regime among 42 countries that controls the export of conventional arms and dual-use goods and technologies, including certain cybersecurity tools. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Remember that encryption exports are regulated. A U.S. company cannot freely export strong encryption to all countries without proper licensing.

items: COBIT — IT governance framework (ISACA); maps business goals to IT goals
ITIL — IT service management best practices
ISO 27001 — Information Security Management System (ISMS) standard; certifiable
NIST CSF — Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover)
FedRAMP — Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program for cloud services

blocks.text: NIST CSF Five Functions: Identify → Protect → Detect → Respond → Recover From Destination CISSP: "FedRAMP has three impact levels (low, moderate, and high) to account for different levels of sensitivity and classification of federal data." ISO 27001 is the only framework in this list that provides organizational certification. Companies can be "ISO 27001 certified," meaning an external auditor has verified their ISMS. ⚠️ Exam Trap: NIST CSF is voluntary and risk-based. ISO 27001 is certifiable. COBIT focuses on governance (linking IT to business). Don't confuse their scopes.
